title: Define customer-facing impact + messaging for KV cache compaction (runtime-1.22)
creator: Nikhil Sharma
description:
Goal
Define customer-facing messaging for the KV cache compaction + eviction work landing in runtime-1.22. This ticket is specifically about: (1) what customers should expect to improve, (2) how we describe it in plain language without over-promising, and (3) tier/config implications for Hosted vs Dedicated (and what Support/CS should say during rollout).

Context (problem we’re solving)
Some customers see burst-driven p95/p99 latency spikes and occasional OOM/request shedding in sustained decode workloads with mixed sequence lengths. Root cause is often KV cache allocator fragmentation under churn: long-lived allocations + frequent request turnover leave the KV arena fragmented, increasing allocator overhead and causing opportunistic evictions at the worst time.

What is shipping (customer-level framing)
Runtime-1.22 introduces “KV cache compaction” (internal name) to keep GPU KV memory more contiguous under load. The system can (a) incrementally compact KV allocations within a controlled budget and (b) evict lower-priority cached state when fragmentation/capacity pressure risks tail latency spikes.

Customer-facing benefits (expected, with caveats)
We should frame benefits as tail-latency stability + fewer pathological events, not raw speedups in every workload.

Primary benefits we can credibly claim:
- Reduced p95/p99 spikes during burst traffic and mixed prompt-length distributions (more predictable decode under churn).
- Lower likelihood of “sudden” latency cliffs caused by fragmentation-triggered allocator/defrag work.
- Fewer rare OOM-driven request sheds in high-churn workloads (not a guarantee; depends on headroom + request patterns).

What we should NOT claim:
- Universal throughput increases. In some regimes there’s a small copy/housekeeping cost; the point is stability under load.
- “No more evictions” or “no more OOM.” We’re adding a safer, more controllable eviction path, not removing all capacity limits.

Quantitative guidance (internal numbers for Sales/CS; not for public docs)
Use ranges and qualify with “in our perf canary / benchmark harness” and “workload dependent.”
- Mixed-length burst scenario (perf canary): p99 end-to-end latency spikes reduced ~20–40% vs runtime-1.21 baseline when fragmentation ratio crosses trigger threshold.
- High-churn chat sessions (staging load test): ~30–60% reduction in time spent in allocator slow paths during sustained decode windows; OOM incidents reduced materially when budgets set conservatively.
- Steady-state throughput: target is within ±1–2% of baseline on common hosted profiles; Dedicated may accept up to ~3% throughput trade for improved p99 depending on chosen budget.

Tier/config implications
Hosted API:
- Default behavior: enabled behind a feature flag with conservative compaction budgets to protect median latency.
- Rollout: staged by cohort/model; we may keep it off for specific models/GPUs until perf canary thresholds are clean.
- Customer messaging: “improves tail-latency stability under bursts; no action required.”
- Support guidance: if a customer reports new latency spikes correlated with compaction metrics, oncall can disable via kill-switch; customer does not need to change anything.

Dedicated:
- Default behavior: enabled for new pools once canary gates pass; existing pools may be opt-in initially depending on contract/SLO sensitivity.
- Config knobs (not customer self-serve in Console for initial release): compaction budget, fragmentation trigger threshold, eviction aggressiveness (tier-aware). Config changes go through Support/Solutions Engineering + SRE guardrails.
- Customer messaging: “improves stability during bursts; if you run very bursty traffic we can tune compaction policy for your pool.”

Private (VPC / on-prem):
- Out of scope for initial customer UI; include a brief note for enterprise roadmap conversations: feature is part of runtime-1.22 and will be available when they pick up that runtime version; tuning available via config.

Eviction policy messaging (important)
We should proactively clarify that eviction affects cached KV state, not correctness:
- Eviction may cause some requests to lose cached state (e.g., prefix cache / continuation) and re-compute tokens, which can increase latency for those specific sequences.
- The policy is tier-aware and avoids pinned sessions; it prioritizes overall system stability.

Proposed customer-facing copy (draft)
Release notes / changelog (internal + customer-facing):
“Runtime 1.22 includes improvements to KV cache memory management designed to reduce tail-latency spikes under bursty, mixed-length workloads. The runtime can now compact fragmented KV allocations within a controlled budget and apply safer, tier-aware eviction under memory pressure. Customers should see more stable p95/p99 latency during bursts with no action required.”

Support macro (for tickets like burst tail latency):
“We’ve shipped runtime-side KV cache memory management improvements that reduce fragmentation-related tail latency spikes under churn. We can confirm whether your pool/cohort has the feature enabled and review compaction/eviction metrics alongside traces. If needed we can adjust the compaction budget/thresholds or disable via a kill-switch while we investigate.”

FAQ bullets for Sales/CS
- Does this change outputs? No; it changes memory management. In some cases evictions can remove cached context, which can increase compute for that request but does not change correctness.
- Does it require customer changes? Hosted: no. Dedicated: optional tuning via Redwood.
- Is this a new SKU? No.
- Is there risk? Yes—overly aggressive compaction can add copy overhead; rollout includes guardrails, automated rollback, and a kill-switch.

Deliverables
1) Final customer-facing release note text for runtime-1.22 (align with ENG-4829 / release train).
2) One-pager for Support/CS: what improved, what metrics to check, what levers exist (budget/threshold/kill-switch), and how to set expectations.
3) Dedicated guidance snippet for Solutions Engineering: when to recommend tuning and what questions to ask (traffic shape, session length, burst patterns).

Open questions to resolve with Eng/SRE (blockers)
- What are the default compaction budgets by tier/model profile in runtime-1.22 canary?
- What metric names will be customer-visible (if any) vs internal-only?
- Confirm automated rollback criteria wording (PM-612) so we don’t contradict oncall policy.
- Confirm whether eviction can affect prefix-cache hit rate materially in common chat workloads (needs a crisp sentence).

Messaging explicitly states workload-dependent impact and does not promise universal throughput gains

updates: 2026-01-16 (Nikhil Sharma): Drafted initial customer framing. Main push is “tail stability under burst + fewer pathological events.” Avoid claiming throughput wins. Waiting on Eng to confirm default budgets/thresholds for Hosted vs Dedicated cohorts.

2026-01-24 (Nikhil Sharma): Synced with Sean/Allison—SRE wants explicit language that compaction is budgeted and can be disabled. Added support macro draft and noted kill-switch policy will reference PM-612.

2026-02-03 (Nikhil Sharma): Lauren requested a Dedicated-specific paragraph: ‘tunable per pool, Redwood-assisted, no Console UI initially.’ Added FAQ about prefix-cache interaction; pending confirmation from Omar on expected hit-rate impact.
2026-02-12 (Nikhil Sharma): Incorporated early perf canary range guidance (keep internal). Next: finalize release note text with Connor (release train) once runtime-1.22 notes are locked.
comments: 2026-01-18 (Sean Gallagher): Please keep the “more stable p99” claim qualified with ‘under burst/mixed-length workloads.’ Also include a sentence that compaction is rate-limited to avoid median latency regressions. We need the support macro to say ‘we can disable quickly’ but not imply it’s unstable by default.

2026-01-22 (Omar El-Sayed): Eviction is tier-aware LRU; pinned sessions shouldn’t be impacted. Prefix cache interaction: eviction can reduce hit rate when memory pressure is high, but this is preferable to global OOM/latency cliffs. Suggest wording: ‘may reduce cache hit rate for some sessions during extreme memory pressure.’

2026-01-29 (Lauren Bishop): Dedicated customers will ask ‘can we tune it?’—answer should be yes via Redwood. Make it explicit that there’s no pricing change and no new SKU; it’s a runtime behavior improvement.

2026-02-06 (Allison Grant): Please don’t include raw metric names in customer-facing release notes; keep those for internal dashboards/runbooks. For CS one-pager, it’s fine to reference ‘fragmentation ratio’ and ‘bytes moved’ as internal signals.
